title: Agentic Engineering in Action with Mitchell Hashimoto
summary: Mitchell Hashimoto walks through a real Ghostty fix done with Claude Code, acting as architect, cleaning up output, and noting where agents excel and where they are hopeless.

assertions.quote: I'm more or less like the architect of the software project.

verdicts.note: Humans still own constraints and tradeoffs, but models can now propose reasonable designs when given context; the gap is narrowing.

assertions.quote: the more vague and the longer you let AI spend on something, uh, the more of a mess it's going to make

verdicts.note: Ignoring code entirely leads to drift and debt in real codebases; but spec-driven approaches with code review do work.

assertions.quote: I think that all the agents are really good at refactoring.

verdicts.note: Refactoring is a relative strength, but studies of LLM refactorings still find behavior-changing errors, so tests or review remain needed.

AI-co-authored commits fix about as many lint-level code smells as they introduce (439,817 vs 432,748), which the authors take as effective local cleanup; this shows smell removal, not reliability on specific refactorings like extracting functions.
Observational: 72% of AI-devs resolved the Bumpy Road smell vs 46% without AI, but AI-devs fully removed Complex Method smells less often (18% vs 32%); assistants, not agents.

Google: 87% of AI JUnit-migration code landed unchanged and the Joda migration saved about 89% of time on small clusters, but in the int64 migration humans usually reverted some changes and messy tests needed human fixes.

Airbnb automated 97% of a 3.5K-file test-framework migration while preserving test intent and coverage, but only with validation gates, many retries and heavy context, so a single pass is not reliable.

assertions.quote: anything more than trivial changes to Zig code bases. Like it's still hopeless uh with that language.

verdicts.note: Model quality tracks training-data volume; benchmarks such as MultiPL-E show much lower scores in less common languages.

assertions.quote: I only find it effective and efficient to use these agentic processes for mid to junior level problems.

verdicts.note: Benchmarks and field studies show strong performance on well-specified, common tasks and weaker results on context-heavy, novel logic.

assertions.quote: what tool have you ever adopted where you were immediately faster.

verdicts.note: Learning curves are real (METR's one dev with >50h Cursor experience was faster), but evidence that ramp-up reliably flips results is thin.

assertions.quote: oh, I actually forgot to update the code. Um, so it's found bugs that way.

verdicts.note: AI reviewers do catch real defects missed by humans, though with notable false-positive rates; complement, not replacement.

assertions.quote: they can't operate in parallel in the same folder

verdicts.note: Shared files and databases cause collisions; worktrees or containers per agent are the standard approach, and Codex and Claude apps build this in.

assertions.quote: it's like shockingly good at this sort of multimodal like here's a picture and reproduce it in Swift UI.

verdicts.note: Screenshot-to-code benchmarks show strong layout reproduction for common components, with fidelity dropping for complex or custom interfaces.

assertions.quote: still challenge yourself to understand how that works even if you're not going to write it

verdicts.note: Studies show novices accept incorrect AI code more often; verifying output requires domain and code literacy.
